https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corp said they will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States meets Tehran’s conditions, including compensation for war damages. The IRGC said their strategy was to maintain the closure “until the enemy accepts all our conditions ... the strait is now actually a theatre of war for us and not just a waterway”. Iran’s security chief Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr on Saturday laid out a list of demands for reopening the strait, including an end to the “war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq”. He also demanded the lifting of a US counterblockade of Iranian ports, the end of sanctions, the release of frozen assets and compensation for wartime damage, according to remarks reported by the Tasnim news agency. Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait since the US and Israel attacked in late February, and wants to charge tolls for passage, striking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its prefer

Photograph: Icac Independent Commission Against Corruption Charles Perrottet becomes Icac’s main character amid claims of hidden payments and political hit jobs The brother of former premier questioned over what, if anything, was done in return for $2m from developer turned fugitive Jean Nassif Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Anne Davies Fri 28 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Finally, we are hearing from one of the central characters, Charles Perrottet, in a saga that has occupied the Independent Commission against Corruption (Icac) for nearly four years. It began with the dismissal of the Hills Shire council and a late night 2022 speech in NSW parliament alleging secret payments from a developer. It pirouetted to a pressure campaign allegedly to remove the then NSW building commissioner, and ended with real world impacts: defective high-rise buildings and thousands of unhappy homebuyers, with the developer nowhere to be seen. Charles Perrottet, brother of the former NSW premier, Dominic Perrottet, finally began giving evidence late Friday. He told the commission that he had met the Toplace developer, Jean Nassif, now a fugitive in Lebanon, in December 2019 and had, over several years, provided him with advice on how to progress his developments. Charles and Nassif bonded over their “frustrations” with David Elliott, the former member for Baulkham Hills, and a key figure in the rival centre-right faction of the Liberals, Charles told Icac. ‘We execute the prick’: Charles Perrottet sent text plotting downfall of NSW Liberal minister, Icac hears Read more “He was frustrated with a number of things. I would listen to him, I would appease him, because I wanted information from him,” Charles said. Elliott had opposed some of Nassif’s developments in the Hills Shire area, earning the developer’s ire. Charles, for his part, was angry about Elliott’s attempts to unseat his brother Dominic and was looking for information on him. Despite having a full-time job at BP as head of strategy, Charles was remunerated for his advice, though not directly. “Jeremy [Greenwood, one of the Reformers] wanted to know if I wanted to share in their success,” Charles Perrottet said. “I said, I have a full-time job. I didn’t want to be paid. I said, you can continue to pay Anita [Perrottet’s wife] and look after her.” View image in fullscreen Sydney property developer Jean Nassif, who is now a fugitive in Lebanon. Photograph: NSW police/AAP Icac is investigating whether Nassif paid $2m in an undeclared political donation to a group of Liberal-aligned conservative men known as the Reformers, including Greenwood and Christian Ellis , in the pursuit of certain political outcomes. In the first weeks of its investigation it focused on how these allegedly illegal donations were allegedly used to fund this group and stack branches with highly conservative members, and ultimately shift the Liberal party to the right. Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads But this week the inquiry has focused on a potentially far more serious issue from a public policy perspective: what, if anything, was done, primarily by Charles Perrottet, for the $2m from Nassif? People like Charles Perrottet are not registered lobbyists. They do not appear in ministerial diaries because meetings on “political matters” with ministers do not have to be disclosed. They can engage casually with key ministerial staff because meetings with staff don’t need to be disclosed anywhere. Many of those working for ministers have their own ambitions within the party and would be flattered by the attention. First the good news: Icac works, but slowly The inquiry might have taken four years to get off the ground but now we are seeing why. Icac is painstakingly testing allegations of hidden payments made to Liberal operatives allegedly for consulting, and outcomes that were either delivered or sought from the Perrottet government. Icac has gone through phone records, text messages, WhatsApp messages, mobile phone tower information, bank records, computers, tax returns and flight records, to track the movements of the key players and the money flow. They even obtained CCTV footage of the main persons of interest meeting up in a hotel. More challenging is establishing whether there is any nexus between payments and political outcomes. View image in fullscreen David Chandler speaks to the media at a building site in Sydney in 2023. Photograph: Jenny Evans/AAP Former builder commissioner David Chandler gave evidence this week of a whisper campaign, which he believed was aimed at ministers and the media, to have him removed. Chandler, a 40-year veteran of the construction industry, is not under investigation by Icac. A former minister, Eleni Petinos, gave evidence that she believed she was “used” in that campaign. She also said she believed she was sacked precipitously by the premier and that she thought there was something else at play. Petinos is not under investigation by Icac. We’ve also heard about Hills Shire Liberal councillors being disendorsed and replaced by a committee of the state executive of the Liberal party. Charles Perrottet and other Reformers occupied key positions on the committee. The old Hills council had been opposing a Toplace development at Cherrybrook. And of course Elliott lost his seat in parliament. Conflicts of interests The Reformers and others involved, like Anita Perrottet, deny that these payments were nefarious and argue instead that they actually did real consulting or lobbying work. Charles Perrottet’s wife, Anita Perrottet, was paid $313,500 from lobbying company Beckington for 18 months in 2021 and 2022 for Greyhounds NSW work and $347,000 in 2022 in “project consulting fees” in the space of three months, “for being a sounding board” for Greenwood and JPG Advisory on Catholic Cemeteries Trust. “That’s $660,999, that’s an enormous amount of money?” said counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC. “I believe that is what I was worth. Jeremy believed I was a huge value-add,” Anita replied. View image in fullscreen Anita Perrottet gives evidence at an Icac hearing on Friday. Photograph: Icac/AAP Anita Perrottet nominated three clients: Greyhounds NSW, while engaged by Beckington, and Catholic Cemeteries Trust and a vaping company, whose name she could not recall, for JPG Advisory, “A sounding board on what?” Dwyer asked. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Five Great Reads Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning after newsletter promotion Anita said her advice was entirely oral and delivered during face-to-face meetings with Greenwood or using her husband’s phone. But she “could not recall” a single detail of her advice. By the end of her two days in the witness box she had said the phrase more than 500 times. Icac has been unable to uncover a single document relating to these clients other than invoices issued by Anita’s company, Macquarie Consulting. No research, emails, marketing strategies or even a text were uncovered. This was 2022, the same time as the NSW premier Dominic Perrottet and his cabinet were debating whether to merge the Catholic-owned cemeteries with the state-owned cemeteries. The Catholic Cemeteries Trust was vigorously resisting the merger. The Catholic Cemeteries Trust was very successful. Despite the issue coming before cabinet several times during 2021 and 2022 and an independent report describing the situation as urgent, the Perrottet government declined to act. Dominic Perrottet did not respond to requests for comment regarding disclosures of family ties to cabinet. Do you know Jean Nassif? At first Anita Perrottet denied that she knew Jean Nassif or that Toplace was a client. But in true Icac style, the bomb was about to drop. She was shown texts about a lunch at Nassif’s house. She said she didn’t remember her husband attending the lunch, but was shown photographs of her children playing at Nassif’s house and texts showing she suggested her husband pick up a bottle of wine to take. Anita was shown a detailed email she allegedly sent to Antony Anisse at another Liberal-aligned lobbying firm, Premier National, regarding a Toplace development in Epsom Road, Rosebery, Dominic Perrottet’s brother allegedly shared ‘dirt’ including secret phone recording of minister, Icac hears Read more The development was facing delays in getting its final occupancy certificate and the email purported to outline an eight-point plan to overcome the difficulties. Anita was unable to say even what some of the acronyms she had allegedly used meant. Dwyer put to Anita that she was being put in “an impossible position” and that she was attempting to cover for her husband, who in fact, was working for Nassif. Anita denied she was lying. “It was a transparent attempt to create a cover for a sham arrangement that had been established by Charles,” Dwyer said. “No,” said Anita. ‘You understand that there is an offence committed if you lie to Icac,” Dwyer said. “Yes,” Anita said. What did the premier know about his brother When he appeared at Icac, former cabinet minister David Elliott described Dominic and Charles Perrottet’s relationship as “joined at the hip”. Dominic Perrotet is not a person of interest. Chandler gave evidence that Dominic Perrottet had begged him to stay on as commissioner, which was exactly the opposite of what Nassif wanted. “I went up and had a cup of tea with the premier and he said: “David, you’ve heard the sentiment of the members and myself and we would like you to reconsider,” he told Icac this week. View image in fullscreen Dominic Perrottet speaks to the media in Parramatta in 2023. Photograph: Louise Kennerley/AAP On the other hand we saw texts that indicate Charles was intimately involved in securing the NSW premiership for his brother. In October 2021, Dominic Perrottet became premier after the surprise resignation of Gladys Berejiklian. In the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Friday we got a rare glimpse into the frantic manoeuvreing to secure him the leadership and the key people involved in the number wrangling. One was Charles Perrottet, the NSW Liberal party right-faction power broker and younger of Dominic, Icac heard. In text messages he and his wife, Anita, discussed his role: “Well, it’s definitely true that he couldn’t have done it without you!!” Anita texted. “But hopefully, you can work together now and going forward to both achieve your goals. Does he feel bad about Kean?” Charles replied: “Yep, I told him what he needs to do there.” Matt Kean had had an agreement with Dominic to become his deputy leader, in return for delivering moderate votes, but ultimately appointed Stuart Ayres. They also discussed pushing council matters with the premier, and also getting rid of David Elliott . “That’s a call for tomorrow. I told him to turn his phone off and savour the moment with Helen, as tomorrow and Tuesday is going to be crucial in showing unity, we execute the prick as soon as party room is over.” Explore more on these topics Independent Commission Against Corruption New South Wales politics Liberal party New South Wales Australian politics features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘We execute the prick’: Charles Perrottet sent text plotting downfall of NSW Liberal minister, Icac hears Teen boy allegedly messaged two others to join ‘degrading’ and ‘humiliating’ Sydney gang-rape, court hears One Nation’s new NSW leader Mike Newman is an investment banker who wants to ‘get rid of wokery’ Bondi library returns book How to Sell a Genocide to shelves after State Library ‘outlines the law’ ‘If you harm my project, I’ll harm you’: former NSW official tells Icac about fugitive developer’s call Dominic Perrottet’s sister-in-law denies lying under oath to protect husband over allegedly illegal donations, Icac hears Police investigate death of teenage girl two days after alleged ‘sexual choking’ act in Sydney Dominic Perrottet’s brother allegedly shared ‘dirt’ including secret phone recording of minister, Icac hears Cults, setups and rumours: years after their downfalls, former NSW Liberal MPs are exacting revenge Now you seafood, now you don’t: $350k worth of oysters vanish without a trace in NSW Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-publi.text: BRUSSELS — The EU wants to transform public procurement into a powerful tool of industrial policy by channeling hundreds of billions of euros spent on infrastructure, schools, energy or health toward European businesses. In its Public Procurement Act unveiled on Wednesday, Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission is following up on recommendations by economic reform guru Mario Draghi to give a lift to struggling European industry while shielding the bloc from external risks in an increasingly uncertain world. The sums involved are huge. Public procurement represents up to 15 percent of the EU’s GDP — or around €2.5 trillion a year. Of that, some €600 billion is governed by EU rules, Executive Vice President Stéphane Séjourné told reporters. Advertisement Advertisement “This is public money, which must also serve our collective goals,” the French commissioner said. “It’s the equivalent of a yearly recovery plan and about four to five times the EU budget in terms of spending.” The Commission is also promising annual cost savings of €650 million for public authorities as three old directives and two dozen sectoral laws — spanning 900 pages — are boiled down into a single regulation running to just 200 pages. That ties in with von der Leyen’s broader second-term agenda of cutting red tape through a series of “omnibus” administrative reforms. To harness public procurement to its strategic goal of strengthening European industry, the EU executive is betting on quality as the main driver in the awarding of public tenders. This would set a minimum quality weighting of 30 percent, rising to 50 percent for labor-intensive contracts. Environmental, social, innovation, security and resilience considerations would all count as quality. Public authorities could still deviate from the rule if they can justify using price alone on the grounds that quality is guaranteed through technical specifications. While public authorities can already put green or social criteria at the center of procurement, Commission research found that their use was neither optimal nor consistent across the bloc. Some contracting authorities, for example, fear litigation if they turn down the lowest-price offer. European preference The proposal also spells out how public authorities can favor EU goods and services — a power that they enjoy under existing rules but rarely use. Under the new rules, authorities could restrict participation, impose origin requirements, and reject tenders where EU or “covered” content accounts for less than 50 percent of the tender’s value. Advertisement Advertisement The Commission’s goal is to provide greater clarity regarding how these rules are applied so that authorities can better evaluate European bids and, if necessary, exclude bids from non-covered countries, Séjourné said. “In any case, it won’t be the European Commissioner’s fault if public procurement agencies choose Chinese buses over European ones, since everything is spelled out in the text and currently allows for the preference of European buses,” he added. Goods that are covered by origin rules in other proposals, such as the Industrial Accelerator Act or the Critical Medicines Act would have to comply with both sets of rules. Stealth omnibus Séjourné described the procurement bill as “an act of radical simplification.” The Commission chose a regulation instead of a directive — over the objections of a majority of member countries. A regulation reduces the scope for divergent national transposition of EU procurement rules, making implementation in national law simpler and avoiding “gold-plating” by capitals. The Public Procurement Act would also make it easier for companies to find and participate in tenders across the EU by introducing a network of digital platforms. There are currently 123 platforms across the bloc — either at national or at local level — and the Commission wants to make sure they all communicate with one another. Different procedures are also simplified and boiled down to two. Advertisement Advertisement The first is a standard, open procedure with offers being assessed before awarding the contract to the winning bid. The second is a “dynamic” procedure where a public authority pools companies that meet its criteria and later invites them to participate in a tender or negotiate for individual procurement opportunities. Procuring innovation The Commission is also seeking to address the longstanding EU problem of homegrown research failing to reach the market. The bloc is a research powerhouse, but innovators and startups often can’t obtain the funding they need in the EU to market their products and scale up within the bloc. They turn to the U.S. for funding instead, or end up in the “valley of death,” which is when a company already has a viable product, but not the funding to market it. The Commission’s answer is its proposed European Innovation Act, also announced on Wednesday, which aims to turn governments into major buyers of pre-commercial solutions. “Innovative ideas developed in Europe too often fail to reach the market, scale across borders or generate new growth sectors,” it states. The Innovation Act has been led by Bulgarian Research Commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva, and was initially more ambitious. But the scope of the law was narrowed down after two negative opinions from the Commission’s quality watchdog, according to documents seen by POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement The EU massively lags other regions in governments procuring research or early-stage prototypes, with the proposal claiming that other regions are investing between five and eight times more than the EU in the public procurement of R&D. One way to correct this is to create an EU-wide framework for pre-commercial procurement. Harmonizing the procedures should also allow for joint procurement by several public buyers across borders. The Innovation Act will also seek to help companies to market their intellectual property, by establishing a new competence center in the EU’s Intellectual Property Office. Finally, the Commission will also come up with a so-called innovation challenge. The idea is to let public authorities start with a problem rather than a product and pitch a “societal challenge” to the market. This article has been updated.

Ukraine: At least 9 people were killed in Russian attacks over the past 24 hours Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 22/10/2026 - 13:11 GMT+2 At least nine people were killed in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past 24 hours, according to Ukrainian authorities, as overnight missile and drone strikes sparked fires in Kyiv and the Kharkiv region. … More In the Kharkiv region , a separate wave of Russian attacks killed one person and injured 15 others , including three children , according to regional governor Oleh Syniehubov. In the city of Kharkiv, drones damaged houses, a shop, cars and an office building , while a strike on a lorry park set four lorries, a trailer and a car on fire. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT In the capital, one person was killed and 22 others injured , including four children , as ballistic missiles and drones struck six districts . Fires broke out in residential and non-residential buildings, while homes, vehicles and infrastructure were damaged . In the Dniprovskyi district , one person was killed and six others, including a child, were injured. Night-time footage shows firefighters tackling blazes from elevated platforms, while images taken after the strikes reveal damaged buildings and burnt-out vehicles . Kyiv’s mayor said debris hit homes and a car service station , with fears that people could be trapped under rubble . Beyond Kyiv and Kharkiv, where one person was killed in each city, Russian attacks also claimed lives in Sumy, Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk , bringing the nationwide death toll to at least nine , according to Ukrainian authorities. The attacks came hours after Moscow and Kyiv agreed in principle to resume US-brokered peace talks . Rescue teams worked through the morning to extinguish fires and assess the damage.
